introduction: The Clothing and Textiles School-Based Assessment requires a practical project - normally one or more constructed items for a named client or for the home - supported by a written folder. The folder records the whole process: research and design ideas, the chosen design with reasons, materials and costing, the production plan or order of work, an illustrated record of construction, and an evaluation of the finished item. Marks are given for the quality of the planning, the skill shown in construction and finishing, the record keeping and the evaluation. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the number of items and the exact format and mark allocation required.

tasks.title: Client and design research
tasks.explanation: Describe the client or user, their needs, the occasion and the purpose of the item, and research the design ideas, fabrics and current fashions that could meet them.

tasks.title: Design presentation
tasks.explanation: Present at least three labelled design ideas (sketches or flats) with fabric swatches, colour schemes and trimmings, and justify the one chosen with reference to design elements and principles.

tasks.title: Production plan and cost sheet
tasks.explanation: Set out the pattern, measurements, materials and trims; cost the item on a cost sheet; list the order of work with a time plan; and describe the safety measures to be taken.

tasks.title: Record of work
tasks.explanation: Record each stage of construction with photographs, samples or sketches - pattern adjustment, cutting, marking, seams, neatening, features, fastenings, hem and pressing - showing techniques and problems solved.

tasks.title: The made item
tasks.explanation: Produce the item to a high standard of sewing, fit, safety, cleanliness, pressing and final finish, inside and out.

tasks.title: Evaluation and recommendations
tasks.explanation: Evaluate the finished item against the client's needs and the design intention, comment on the standard of your own work, identity faults and their causes, and recommend improvements.

sampleTitle: A reversible summer dress for a twelve-year-old using madras cotton

sample.body: The client is a growing twelve-year-old who needs a cool dress for church and school functions that will not date quickly. Three ideas were sketched: a pinafore with a buttoned bodice, a gathered sundress with a band, and a simple A-line shift with a faced neckline and pockets. The shift was chosen because its vertical seams and A-line give a lengthening effect and allowance for growth, because the princess seams avoid a waistline that would be outgrown in a term, and because madras cotton - a plain weave, absorbent, washable, bright and traditional - suits the hot climate and shows the pattern to advantage. The madras check provides rhythm through repetition; the plain back panel was chosen so that the check does not clash at a centre back seam.
sample.tips: Name the design element and principle in each reason, and always link a property of the fabric to a need of the client.

sample.body: The dress fits and is comfortable, and the client wears it often, so the design aim was met. The seams pressed open cleanly and the faced neckline sits flat, but two faults remain: the left side seam is slightly puckered because the stitch length was too long for the fine cotton, and the hem is one centimetre lower at the back because the hem was levelled before the client tried it on. Marks were lost on the inside finish, where the raw edges of the darts were not neatened. Improvements: shorten the stitch length for lightweight cotton, level hems with the garment on the client, and neaten every raw edge before the final press. If repeated, the pattern would be cut with slightly larger seam allowances to allow letting out as the child grows.
sample.tips: Identify real faults, name their cause and give a specific, technical remedy - vague praise loses evaluation marks.

marking: Marks reward thorough research, well-presented and justified designs, accurate planning and costing, a clear illustrated record of work, a practical item that shows good technique and a professional finish, and a candid evaluation that identifies faults and recommends improvements.

The client, the wearer, the shops, the measurements, the prices and the times are invented to show what a full-mark Clothing and Textiles folder looks like. Read it, study how the design is justified, how the cost sheet is built and how the faults are written up, then produce your own garment for your own client. This sample cannot be copied.

categories.comment: The client, the wearer, the five needs and the three occasions are recorded from a real interview, with the measurements taken twice, a priced survey of three comparable shop dresses checked against the tickets, four fabrics handled and washed before choosing, and shrinkage and colour bleeding tested rather than assumed.

Three labelled ideas are presented with their fabric, trims, cost and time, the two rejected ones with the wearer's own objection; the chosen reversible A-line is justified by naming rhythm and repetition, balance, proportion, emphasis and harmony, and the whole specification it must meet is written out.

The pattern pieces, the cut list of 17 pieces, the fabric layout with the 0.25 m plaid matching allowance, the order of work with a time plan against actual times, a cost sheet showing materials, labour and overheads, and eight named safety measures with the sample seams that set the stitch length.

Ten stages are recorded with the technique named at each one - plain seams pressed open, grading, pinking, clipping, under-stitching, turning through, patch pockets, buttonholes through two layers, shanks, binding a hem and levelling on the wearer - with the machine settings, the photographs and the cut sample of every seam.

The finished dress meets ten of the eleven points of its own specification exactly, with the length changed by 3 cm at the client's request and recorded as a change; ten quality checks cover reversibility, plaid matching, seam standard, binding, buttons, pockets, press and comfort, with the one imperfect point named.

The four faults are recorded with place, cause, remedy and the minutes each cost, the time overrun and the money saved are both explained rather than just reported, the saving is honestly attributed to unpaid making, and seven specific improvements are given with the client's and the wearer's own comments used as evidence.

pages.heading: Cover page and contents
pages.body: This is the folder for my CSEC Clothing and Textiles School-Based Assessment project: a reversible A-line summer dress made for Kimone Dixon, aged 12 (invented), the daughter of Mrs Marlene Dixon (invented), of Sample Village. The dress is made in madras cotton plaid on one side and plain white cotton poplin on the other, so the client's daughter has two dresses in one and the plaid side can be worn to church while the plain side is worn to the beach. The client, her daughter, the school, the shops surveyed and every measurement, price and time in this folder are invented for this worked example; they do not describe a real client or a real purchase. The folder holds 23 sections: the research into the client and the fabric, the three design ideas with the one chosen, the plan and the cost sheet, the record of construction with the faults found and put right, the measurements and quality checks on the finished dress, and an evaluation against the client's needs. The item itself is submitted with the folder, together with the pattern, the sample seams, the fabric swatches and the care card given to the client.

pages.heading: Research: the client, her daughter and the occasion
pages.body: I wrote to Mrs Marlene Dixon (invented) and asked for an interview, and she invited me to her home on a Saturday morning with her daughter Kimone Dixon, aged 12 (invented) present. The interview lasted about forty minutes and I made notes and took the measurements in the same visit, so the figures in this folder were taken from the person who would wear the dress and not from a size chart. The client's daughter is twelve years old and still growing: she had gone up two dress sizes in the previous year, so anything tight at the waist would be outgrown in a term. She needs a cool dress for church, for school functions and for the beach, and the client asked for one garment that would do all three rather than three garments. The family washes by hand in cool water and dries clothes on a line in the sun, and the client does not want a garment that has to be dry-cleaned or ironed with care. The daughter dresses herself and asked for a dress she can put on and take off without help, which rules out a back zip and rules in a loose pull-on shape with fastenings she can reach. She also wanted pockets, because she carries a phone and a handkerchief to church. The client's last point was the one that shaped the whole design: her daughter dislikes wearing the same dress to two events in the same month, so the client asked whether one dress could be made to look like two. That is where the idea of a reversible dress came from, and the client set a budget of 3,500.00 for materials and a deadline of the school's prize-giving service.

pages.heading: Research: the measurements taken and how they were checked
pages.body: The measurements in the table were taken over the daughter's underclothes with a dressmaker's tape, standing up straight with her arms down. Each measurement was taken twice and the two readings agreed to within half a centimetre; the tape was checked against a metre rule before I started, because a stretched tape would have thrown every figure in the folder out by the same amount. Ease was then added on top of the body measurements, and the amount of ease is shown for each measure so that the pattern drafting in section 10 can be checked against it. The ease is generous for two reasons: the daughter is growing, and the two layers of the reversible dress take up room inside the garment that a single layer would not. The finished hem circumference of 120.0 cm is the one measurement that the design sets rather than the body: it is 34.0 cm more than the hip measurement, which gives the A-line its swing and lets the dress be pulled on over the head without a fastening. The planned dress length of 80.0 cm from the shoulder was measured on the daughter in front of a mirror and it came to just below the knee; the finished dress measures 77.0 cm because the client asked for 3 cm to be taken off at the second fitting.

pages.heading: Research: what ready-made dresses cost and what they do not solve
pages.body: The client had already looked at dresses in the shops and she gave me the prices she had been quoted, which I wrote down and then checked against the price tickets on a visit to the same three shops on a Saturday afternoon. The three garments are described in the table below. They cost between 6,500.00 and 7,200.00, and the average of the three is 6,866.67, which is the figure I use for the saving in the cost sheet in section 11. Price was not the only thing that mattered. None of the three dresses was reversible, so the client's daughter would still need two garments to avoid wearing the same dress to two events; the cheapest of the three was finished with overlocked seams that felt scratchy against the skin; and the market stall dress carried no care label at all, which matters for a family that washes by hand and dries in the sun. Comparing the three also taught me something about how the plaid is used: on the market stall dress the plaid was cut off the grain at the side seams, so the check ran downhill on one side and the dress hung crooked. That is the fault I was most careful to avoid when I laid out the madras in section 10, and it is the fault recorded as the first of the four in section 15.

pages.heading: Research: the fabrics considered and why madras cotton was chosen
pages.body: Three fabrics were considered for the dress and each one was handled, held up to the light and washed in a sample before a decision was made. Madras is the name used in the Caribbean for a light plaid cotton of the kind used for children's wear, shirts and household cloth: it is a plain weave, it is absorbent, it takes a bright dye well and it washes and irons without trouble, which is exactly what a family washing by hand and drying in the sun needs. Its weakness is shrinkage and colour movement in hot water, so both lengths of fabric were washed in cool water and pressed before they were cut, and the madras was measured before and after: it lost about 5.2 cm on a 130 cm length, which is the 4.0 per cent allowance made in the layout. That wash also settled the question of colour: the red in the plaid bled a little into the rinse water on the first wash, which is why the care card tells the client to wash the dress on its own for the first two washes. The plaid itself was chosen as much for design as for comfort. A check gives rhythm and repetition on a plain shape without any trimming being added, and it hides the seams of a growing child's dress better than a plain colour does. The plain white poplin for the reverse side is the same weight and the same 115 cm width, so the two layers behave identically under the machine; a lighter fabric on one side would have shown through and would have made the hems uneven.

pages.heading: Design: the three ideas presented and why two were rejected
pages.body: Three design ideas were drawn as labelled flats on A4 sheets and shown to the client with the fabric swatches pinned to each one, so that she could see how the plaid would sit on the shape rather than imagine it. The flats, the swatches and the client's written comments on each sheet are in the appendix. The client chose the third idea, the reversible A-line dress, and the two rejected ideas are worth recording because they show what the reversible design had to answer. The pinafore was rejected on the wearer's own objection: a pinafore is worn over another garment, so it is not two looks in one and it would not have been cool enough for the beach. The banded sundress was the cheapest and the quickest to make, but the fixed waistband and the elasticated back were the two things most likely to be outgrown within a term, and the client's daughter had grown two sizes in the previous year.

pages.heading: Design: the chosen dress described and justified
pages.body: The chosen dress is an A-line summer dress made twice over: every pattern piece is cut in madras cotton plaid and again in plain white cotton poplin, and the two dresses are joined at the neckline, the armholes and the back opening so that either side can be worn outside. The neckline is a shallow scoop wide enough to pass over the head, the bodice has no waist dart and no waistband, the skirt is cut as an A-line from the waist seam to a hem of 120.0 cm, there is a patch pocket on each side of each front, and the back opening closes with four 12 mm buttons whose buttonholes are worked through both layers, which is the detail that makes the fastening reversible. The garment is finished with 1350 mm wide bias binding around the hem. The design is justified by naming the element and the principle in each reason. The madras check provides rhythm and repetition: the repeated squares lead the eye down the length of the dress without any trimming being added. The dress is symmetrical about the centre front, which gives balance as well as making the pockets easy to place. Proportion is controlled by dividing the length into three parts - roughly a third for the bodice, a third for the skirt above the knee and a third for the hem sweep - so the dress does not look short-waisted. Emphasis falls on the plaid, which is why the plain side is kept completely plain and the binding is cut from the plaid: on the plain side the piped edge is the one line of colour. Harmony comes from using the same madras for the pockets on both sides, so whichever way the dress is worn there is a square of plaid to look at. The A-line shape and the 1.5 cm seam allowances are the growth allowance the client asked for, and the reversible construction means one garment covers two occasions, which was the client's main need.

pages.heading: Method: how the folder was organised and the project worked through
pages.body: The project ran from the first letter to the client to the second fitting and took 12 workshop sessions of 90 minutes plus drafting and finishing at home. The folder is organised in the order the work was actually done, so the plan in section 9 can be read against the construction record in section 13 and the faults in section 15. The method was as follows. First, the client was found and interviewed, and the wearer was measured; the letter, the interview notes and the measurements are the evidence for the research sections. Second, three design ideas were drawn as labelled flats, fabric swatches were pinned to each sheet and the client chose one in writing. Third, the measurements were turned into a paper pattern with 1.5 cm seam allowances and the bodice was tested as a toile in calico before any good fabric was touched, which is where the first correction (below) came from. Fourth, the fabric was washed, dried and pressed and then cut, with the plaid laid so that the horizontal and vertical lines of the check ran true to the grain and matched at the centre back. Fifth, the item was constructed in the order set out in section 9, and each stage was photographed and the machine setting written down as it was done, with a cut sample of every seam kept and stapled into the record. Sixth, the faults found were written up with their causes and remedies immediately, including the three that cost extra time, and the dress was re-checked against the specification in section 7 after they were put right. Finally, the finished dress was fitted twice, photographed inside and out, measured against the specification and evaluated against the client's needs, and the client was given the care card, the leftover binding and the pattern in case a second dress is wanted.

pages.heading: Planning: the order of work and the time plan
pages.body: The order of work below is the sequence the dress was actually made in, written before the fabric was cut and then kept up to as the work went on. The order matters as much as the times: the toile has to be tested before the good fabric is cut, the two layers must be pressed at every change of direction or the reversible dress will never sit flat, the hem can only be bound after the length has been checked on the wearer, and the buttonholes must be worked after the two layers are joined, because they have to pass through both. The plan allowed 14 hours 45 minutes across 10 workshop sessions of 90 minutes. The making actually took 17 hours 40 minutes and needed 12 sessions of 90 minutes, so it ran 175 minutes (19.8 per cent) over the plan. The overrun is not a mystery: 95 of those 175 minutes went on putting the four faults right, and all four are written up with their causes in section 15; the remaining 80 minutes went on the ordinary cost of pressing two layers instead of one and on the second fitting. The booked workshop time was 1080 minutes, so the work finished with 20 minutes still spare inside the booked sessions, which is a thin margin and is one of the recommendations in section 21.

pages.heading: Planning: the pattern pieces, the cut list and the fabric layout
pages.body: The pattern was drafted from the measurements in section 3 onto pattern paper, with 1.5 cm seam allowances added to every edge and the grain line marked on each piece. Four pattern pieces were drafted - the front bodice on the fold, the back bodice half, the skirt on the fold and the pocket - and cutting them twice over, once in each fabric, produced the 17 garment pieces listed below. Nothing was cut until the bodice toile had been fitted and corrected, because the first toile was too wide across the chest and the bust ease was reduced by 1 cm before the good fabric was touched. The layout is the part of the plan that earned its keep. Madras cotton is a plaid, so the pieces cannot be laid for economy alone: the horizontal line of the check must run level across the garment and the vertical line must run true to the grain, and the plaid must match where two pieces meet at the centre front, the centre back and the side seams. That is why the madras length needed 1.30 m of cloth while the plain cotton needed only 1.00 m for the same pieces, and why a further 0.25 m of madras is accounted for as matching allowance. Both lengths were washed, dried in the shade and pressed before cutting, and the madras was measured again afterwards.

pages.heading: Planning: the fabric layout and what it allowed for
pages.body: The two layouts are described below. The madras was laid right side up with the selvedges level and the plaid squared with the table edge using a set square and a long ruler, because a plaid laid down slightly on the slant produces a dress that hangs crooked and no amount of pressing will put it right. The two skirt panels went down first, side by side, and the bodice pieces above them, with the pockets and the binding strips fitted into the spaces between them. Pins were put in at right angles to the edges so that they could be felt by hand and the fabric was not lifted off the table; the pieces were cut with long, even strokes of the shears so that the edges did not go into steps. The plain poplin was laid the same way, using the madras pieces as a check that every piece had been cut twice. The unused madras, about 0.20 m of it, went into the class scrap box along with 0.65 m of the bias binding, which is the material the client did not pay for.

pages.heading: Planning: the cost sheet, the budget and the saving
pages.body: The cost sheet sets out materials, labour and overheads separately, as the SBA requires. Materials came to 2,477.00 against the client's budget of 3,500.00, so the client paid 1,023.00 less than she had allowed - she used 70.8 per cent of her budget. Labour is shown at 180.00 an hour and comes to 3,180.00 for 17 hours 40 minutes of making, and overheads are the machine power at 35.00 an hour plus consumables, 798.33 in all. The client was not charged labour or overheads: the making was part of my assessment and it would not be honest to charge a client for a garment I was learning to make. Showing them anyway is the point of the exercise, because it tells the client what a repeat order would really cost. That is why the last two lines of the cost sheet matter. The client paid 2,477.00 for a dress that the shops sell for an average of 6,866.67, a saving of 4,389.67, or 63.9 per cent. But if the labour and the overheads were charged at the rates shown, the dress would cost 6,455.33 and the saving would shrink to 411.34. The honest conclusion is that the saving to this client came from the making being free rather than from the materials being cheap, and that is the figure I would quote to anyone who asked whether a home-made dress saves money.

pages.heading: Planning: equipment, sample seams and safety measures
pages.body: The equipment used was the school's sewing machine, an overlocker for the raw edges of the plain seams, a steam iron and pressing board, dressmaker's shears, small scissors or snips, a tape measure, a metre rule and set square for the plaid, pins, hand needles for the hems and the buttons, tailors' chalk, a tracing wheel and dressmaker's carbon, a bodice stand for the fittings and an ironing cloth or press cloth. Before the good fabric was cut, three sample seams were stitched on the offcuts: a plain seam at 2.5 mm, the same seam pressed open, and a seam pressed to one side to see which behaved better on two layers of cotton. The samples were then washed and pressed and stapled into the record, which is how the stitch length of 2.5 mm with the tension at 4 and a 75/11 needle was settled. The first sample, sewn at 3 mm, puckered on the fine poplin and was rejected. Safety was planned before the first session rather than thought about afterwards, because a workshop with an iron and a machine in it has two obvious dangers.
bullets: Machine: the needle unthreaded and the presser foot down when the machine is left, and the foot off the pedal while pinning
Pins: kept in a magnetic tray, never held in the mouth, and the fabric kept on the table while fingers stay behind the needle
Iron: checked for a frayed flex before use, filled to the mark, stood upright between presses, never left face down on the cloth
Cutting: the shears passed handle first, the table cleared first, and the shears closed and put down when anyone speaks to me
Hands and eyes: fingers kept clear of the needle, no loose sleeves, and the work turned to the light rather than leaning over it
Work area: the floor swept at the end of every session and pins counted back into the tray before anything is thrown away
Electrical: one machine per socket, no trailing leads across the walking route, the iron unplugged at the end of the session and the flex stored loosely
First aid: the kit and the teacher's position known before the first session, and the teacher told whenever a machine is threaded or the iron is moved

pages.heading: Construction record: the making stage by stage
pages.body: The construction record below is written from the notes and the photographs taken at the time, and the cut sample of every seam is stapled beside it in the folder. The step minutes are the same minutes as the order of work in section 9, stage for stage, so the two tables can be read against each other: the stage that overran and the remedy that caused the overrun appear in both. Each step gives the technique by name so that a reader can see which one was used, and the settings were the same throughout unless the table says otherwise. Three of the steps needed unpicking and re-doing, and all three are recorded here as they happened rather than tidied away, with the causes and remedies set out in section 15. Pressing is written into almost every step because in a reversible garment a seam is not finished when it is sewn, it is finished when it is pressed, and each side of the dress shows the same seam from opposite faces. Photographs of the work on the stand at the end of steps 4, 6, 8, 10 and 11 are numbered in the appendix, and the inside of the finished dress is photographed at step 11 as well, so that the standard of the neatening can be judged from the side that will be worn against the skin.

pages.heading: Construction record: the techniques used, named correctly
pages.body: The techniques below are the ones a Clothing and Textiles folder is expected to name, and each is listed with the place it was used and the reason it was chosen for this garment. Naming them correctly matters: a plain seam, a French seam and a run-and-fell seam all close an edge, but only one of them belongs in a reversible garment, and the reason the plain seam was used everywhere is that every seam is visible from one side of this dress and none of them may be uncomfortable against the skin. Similarly, clipping the curve and under-stitching are the two techniques that stop a turned neckline rolling out, and in a reversible dress a rolled edge is visible from both sides at once.

pages.heading: Construction record results: the faults found and the remedies applied
pages.body: Four faults were found during the making, and each one is recorded with where it happened, what caused it and what was done about it. The remedies are written in the order they were carried out, because the sequence matters: the plaid had to be put right before the skirt was cut, and the buttonholes could not be re-worked until the two layers had been tacked together. Three of the four faults are the kind a marker can check, because the evidence is in the folder: the re-cut back bodice is photographed beside the rejected one, the puckered armhole is photographed before it was unpicked, and the buttonholes re-worked through both layers are shown on both faces of the dress in the photographs at steps 10 and 11. The four faults together cost 95 minutes, which is a useful figure to set against the overrun in section 9: 95 of the 175 minutes over the plan went on putting things right, and the remaining 80 minutes went on pressing, clipping and the extra care a reversible garment takes. The one fault I would call serious is the buttonholes, because it could have been avoided by a check that takes seconds: holding the two layers together and pushing a pin through both before the first buttonhole is cut.

pages.heading: Practical results: the finished dress measured against the specification
pages.body: The finished dress was measured against the specification in section 7 and the readings are set out below. Ten of the eleven points measure exactly what the specification asked for. The exception is the length, and it is the one change the client asked for: the skirt came off at the second fitting, so the skirt is 47.0 cm and the dress 77.0 cm from the shoulder rather than the 80.0 cm planned. It is recorded here as a change rather than as a measurement that happens to differ, because a marker cannot tell the difference between a deliberate alteration and a mistake unless the folder says which it was; the second fitting notes and the client's initials against the new length are in the appendix. Everything that could be measured flat was measured twice, and the dress was also worn for the measuring: the flat bust and hip readings are the same as the specification's, and the hem circumference of 120.0 cm was measured around the hem with the dress hanging from the stand so that the sweep was not pulled out of shape.

pages.heading: Practical results: the quality checks on seams, binding, buttons and finish
pages.body: The quality checks were carried out on the finished dress before it was handed over, with the dress on the stand for the outside and turned inside out for the reverse side. The checks are written as a table because a check is only worth anything if it says what was looked at and what was found. Two of them deserve a comment. The reversibility check is the one that decides whether the whole design has worked: the dress was turned over and inspected on both faces, and there is no raw edge, no visible seam allowance and no pucker to be seen from either side, which is what the plain seam pressed open, the pinking and the under-stitching were there to achieve. The plaid check is the one the market stall dress had failed: the horizontal line of the check runs level across the dress and the plaid matches at the centre back and at both side seams, which is what the 0.25 m matching allowance in the layout was spent on. The only point that is not perfect is the inside of the plain side at the pocket corners, where the pinking shows a little on the closest look; it is recorded honestly rather than left out, and the improvement is in section 21.

pages.heading: Practical results: the fittings and what the client and the wearer said
pages.body: There were two fittings, both at the client's home, and the notes from each are in the appendix with the photographs. The first fitting was the toile of the bodice, before any good fabric was cut, and it found the same fault that the second fitting found on the finished dress: the first toile was too wide across the chest, and the bust ease was cut back by 1 cm, which is the reason step 2 of the construction record took 20 minutes longer than planned. The second fitting was the finished dress, worn for twenty minutes while the client's daughter sat, reached and walked, and it produced three pieces of information: the shoulders stayed in place without slipping, the client asked for 3 cm off the length, and the wearer said she would wear the plain side to the beach and the plaid to church. The third comment is the one the design was built for. Both the client and her daughter handled the dress on both faces before the client signed the fitting note, and the wearer's verdict was that the plain side did not look like the inside of a dress, which is the phrase I would keep from the whole project. The client's own comment was about the hem: she said the piped edge made the plain side look finished rather than plain, which is the emphasis the design intended.

pages.heading: Discussion: how the reversible design changed the making
pages.body: Choosing a reversible dress changed almost every decision after the design was agreed, and it is worth setting out what that did to the work, because it is the reason this garment took 17 hours 40 minutes rather than the 14 hours 45 minutes the plan allowed. Every seam was made twice over and every one of them is visible from one side of the garment, so there is no such thing as a hidden seam in this dress. That has three consequences. First, the fabric had to be cut twice with the same care: it is easy to cut a lining quickly when nobody will see it, but the plain poplin side of this dress is a face, not a lining, which is why the plain layer took as long to cut and press as the plaid. Second, the neatening had to be smooth rather than merely strong: an overlocked edge would have ridged through the plain side, so the allowances were pressed open and the edges pinked instead, and the armhole curves were clipped and under-stitched so that neither side rolls out. Third, the fastening had to be worked through both layers, which is the single detail that failed first time round and cost 30 minutes. The plaid made its own demand on top of all this, because a check cannot be cut for economy: the 0.25 m matching allowance in the layout is the price of a dress that hangs straight, and the market stall dress surveyed in section 4 is the proof of what happens when that price is not paid. The design principles were not decoration either: the plain side is kept completely plain so that the one line of plaid in the binding is the emphasis, and the pockets repeat the plaid as squares so that the plain side still carries the rhythm of the check without any of its noise.
bullets: Twice the cutting, twice the seams and twice the pressing for the same garment
No hidden seam: the plain side is a face, not a lining, so both layers were cut and pressed to the same standard
Smooth neatening (pressed open and pinked) instead of overlocking, so no ridge shows through the poplin
The fastening had to pass through both layers, which is where the worst of the four faults happened
The plaid layout cost 0.25 m of extra fabric and bought a dress that hangs straight
The binding carries the plaid on to the plain side and gives it the one line of emphasis the design asked for

pages.heading: Discussion: the cost and the time against the plan
pages.body: The plan allowed 3,500.00 for materials and 14 hours 45 minutes of making, and the project took 2,477.00 and 17 hours 40 minutes. The money came in under the budget by 1,023.00 (70.8 per cent of the budget was used) and the time came in over the plan by 175 minutes, or 19.8 per cent. Both of those figures deserve a comment rather than just being reported. The budget was not exceeded because the two dear materials were bought in measured lengths rather than in whole pieces: the layout in section 10 was worked out on paper, in centimetres, before a metre of fabric was bought, and the 0.25 m plaid matching allowance was the only extra length added beyond what the pieces needed. The unused 0.65 m of bias binding and the leftover madras went back to the class store, and the client is entitled to know that they were not charged to her. The wage side of the cost sheet is where the honest reading is: the client paid 2,477.00 for a dress that the shops price at an average of 6,866.67, a saving of 4,389.67 or 63.9 per cent. But the total cost of production, with labour at 180.00 an hour and overheads at 35.00 an hour, is 6,455.33, which is only 411.34 less than the average shop price. The saving therefore comes from the making being unpaid, as part of my assessment, and not from the materials or from any special skill of mine. The time overrun has the same shape: 95 minutes of the 175 went on putting four faults right, and those four faults were all avoidable with checks that take seconds - checking a repeat before cutting, pinning rather than hoping, and pushing a pin through two layers before cutting a buttonhole. If the dress were made again the two stages that ran over for that reason, cutting the madras and working the buttonholes, would be back inside the plan.

pages.heading: Limitations and improvements
pages.body: The limitations below are stated plainly, because a folder that claims a perfect garment is not believable and does not tell the client what a second dress would need.
bullets: The plan booked 10 workshop sessions and the work needed 12, finishing with only 20 minutes spare inside the booked time, which left no room for a further fault. Improvement: book one whole session as contingency on any project with a plaid to match or a fastening to work through two layers.

The A-line gives growth room at the waist and the hip, but the bodice is cut to a fixed bust measurement, so the dress will need a new bodice if the wearer grows another two sizes. Improvement: cut the bodice with a 2 cm side-seam allowance turned in, so it can be let out once.

The dress has no pockets with a fastening, so the phone the wearer carries can fall out when she sits. Improvement: add a flap or a button to the pocket on the plaid side, and record it as a design change for the client to approve.

The pinking on the plain side of the seams shows a little at the two lower pocket corners. Improvement: use a narrower pinked edge or bind the pocket corners, and photograph the inside as part of the checks next time.

The care card asks for hand washing, because the madras bled slightly on the first wash in the sample. Improvement: wash a larger sample twice and record the colour fastness properly, so the advice given to the client is based on two washes rather than one.

The buttonholes were worked by machine, which is quicker but less forgiving on two layers. Improvement: tack both layers and test the buttonhole on a scrap of the two layers joined before cutting the first real buttonhole.

The pattern is kept, but it was drafted once and corrected by hand at the toile stage. Improvement: redraft the pattern cleanly from the corrected toile before cutting the good fabric, so the pattern handed to the client is accurate if she wants another dress.
The time plan did not allow any contingency for putting faults right. Improvement: add a 30 minute contingency to any stage that involves matching a plaid or working a fastening through two layers.

pages.heading: Conclusion
pages.body: The client asked for one cool dress that would do for church, for school functions and for the beach, that her daughter could put on without help, that would survive a summer of growing, and that would not be the same dress twice in a month. The reversible A-line dress in madras cotton and plain poplin answers all five needs: it is cut in cotton for the heat, it has no fastening further than the four buttons at the centre back, the A-line and the 1.5 cm seam allowances give room to grow, and the two sides give the client's daughter two dresses in one garment. The dress was measured against its own specification after the faults were put right and ten of the eleven points met it exactly, with the eleventh - the length - changed by 3 cm at the client's own request and recorded as a change. The cost sheet shows what the project really cost: 2,477.00 of materials against a budget of 3,500.00, with labour of 3,180.00 and overheads of 798.33 shown but not charged, which is why the client's saving of 4,389.67 should be read as the value of unpaid making rather than as a bargain in the fabric. Four faults were found and all four were put right before the dress was handed over, and if I made the dress again I would check the plaid repeat before cutting, tack the two layers before the first buttonhole, and level the hem on the wearer from the start. The client has the dress, the pattern, the care card and the leftover binding, and she has asked whether the same pattern could be used for a younger cousin in a different plaid.

examinerNotes: This subject is marked out of 60 under six tasks, and the folder answers each one with real work: an interview and measurements, three labelled design ideas, a cost sheet with materials, labour and overheads, an order of work, a construction record with named techniques, a finished garment measured against its own specification, and an evaluation that names its faults.

The strongest feature is that the folder counts. The bust ease of 4 cm, the 120.0 cm hem, the 1.5 cm seam allowances, the 0.25 m plaid matching allowance, the 14 hours 45 minutes plan against 17 hours 40 minutes actual (a 19.8 per cent overrun, of which 95 minutes is the four faults) and the price survey all agree with one another, because every figure in the folder was worked out from one set of measurements instead of being estimated section by section.

Design is justified the way the checklist asks: each reason names the element and the principle - rhythm and repetition from the plaid, balance from the symmetric centre front, proportion from the three-part length, emphasis from the plain side with its one piped line of plaid, and harmony from repeating the plaid in the pockets - and each reason is tied to a need of the client rather than to a taste of the candidate.

The evaluation is candid about money as well as about sewing. It states that the client's 4,389.67 saving comes from the making being unpaid rather than from cheap materials, and that the total cost of production of 6,455.33 is only 411.34 below the average shop price. Client, wearer, school, shops and all figures are invented placeholders; make your own garment for your own client, with your own evidence.
